media:group.media:title: The Wyss Instrumentation Program
media:group.media:description:
The Scientific Instrumentation @ Wyss Collaboratories Program (Wyss Instrumentation Program) is a unique collaboration between industry manufacturers and our community of scientists and engineers to advance discoveries, spur entrepreneurship, and drive impact. At the Wyss, we have a strong record of supporting the advancement of scientific discoveries to real-world impact through commercialization. The Instrumentation Program accelerates this translation by collaborating with budding entrepreneurs on novel applications and the use of cutting-edge equipment that may be uncommon in academic settings but indispensable in industry labs to develop medicines or technologies at scale for our society.
For more information, please visit: https://wyss.harvard.edu/collaboration/scientific-instrumentation-wyss-collaboratories-program/
Credit: Wyss Institute at Harvard University

entry.title: The Importance of Science Part II

media:group.media:title: The Importance of Science Part II
media:group.media:description:
In a follow-up to our first Importance of Science video, we sit down with leaders of patient advocacy foundations, one of our board members, Wyss Lumineers (alumni), and a new set of researchers to reflect on the current climate of the scientific community. We explore how the abrupt changes in government funding for scientific research in 2025 have affected the trajectory of scientific research and the ways researchers have adapted to continue their high-impact work.
Credit: Wyss Institute at Harvard University
For more information, please visit: wyss.harvard.edu

media:group.media:title: 20-ish Questions with Donald E. Ingber
media:group.media:description:
20-ish Questions shows a different side of Wyss Institute faculty, touching on aspects of their personal life, hobbies, interests, as well as their research. This round follows Donald E. Ingber, the Founding Director and a Core Faculty member at the Wyss Institute. He is also the Judah Folkman Professor of Vascular Biology at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children’s Hospital as well as the Hansjörg Wyss Professor of Bioinspired Engineering at the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences.
Ingber is a pioneer in the field of biologically inspired engineering, and at the Wyss Institute, he currently leads scientific and engineering teams that cross a broad range of disciplines to develop breakthrough bioinspired technologies to advance healthcare and improve sustainability. His work has led to major advances in mechanobiology, cell structure, tumor angiogenesis, tissue engineering, systems biology, nanobiotechnology, and translational medicine. Through his work, Ingber has also helped to break down boundaries between science, art and design.
For more information, please visit: https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/executive-team/donald-ingber/
Credit: Wyss Institute at Harvard University

entry.title: Just Published, Now What? with Nayoung Kim and Peter Nguyen

media:group.media:title: Just Published, Now What? with Nayoung Kim and Peter Nguyen
media:group.media:description:
Climate change and human-caused pollution are disrupting ocean ecosystems and reshaping marine biomes, driving pathogen outbreaks, toxin-producing harmful algal blooms, and coral bleaching. Being able to monitor so-called “barometer species” could provide critical insights into the pulse of ocean health, reveal both acute local and long-term global trends, and help drive effective climate change policy, remediation, and stewardship solutions. Researchers at the Wyss Institute and M.I.T. have developed a field-deployable, CRISPR-based biosensing platform that could enable facile, real-time monitoring of marine barometer species and ecosystems.
For more information, please visit: https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/tooling-up-to-diagnose-ocean-health/

media:group.media:description:
20-ish Questions shows a different side of Wyss Institute faculty, touching on aspects of their personal life, hobbies, interests, as well as their research. This round follows Christopher Chen, a Core Faculty member at the Wyss Institute. He is also the William Fairfield Warren Distinguished Professor, Biomedical Engineering & Director, Biological Design Center at Boston University. The goal of Dr. Chen’s research is to identify the underlying mechanisms by which cells interact with materials and each other to build tissues, and to apply this knowledge to the biology and engineering of stem cells, tissue vascularization, connective tissues, and cancer research.
For more information, please visit: https://wyss.harvard.edu/team/core-faculty/christopher-chen/

entry.title: Just Published, Now What? with Justin Rolando

media:group.media:title: Just Published, Now What? with Justin Rolando
media:group.media:description:
As recent outbreaks showed, infection with the pathogenic yeast fungus Candida auris can wreak havoc on the health of hospital patients and residents of nursing homes, especially those who are already weakened by other illnesses. Clinicians need a much more effective diagnostic tools to rapidly and accurately quantify the abundance of the pathogen in patients and assess its antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
A new study, led by David Walt and James Collins, offers a solution to this problem with a new precision diagnostic approach that for the first time enables fast and accurate quantification of C. auris strains from easily obtained swab samples, as well as the quantification of AMR-causing mutations in fungal populations with mixed antifungal susceptibility. dSHERLOCK, how the next-gen diagnostic test is called, was validated with the help of patient samples provided by the Wadsworth Center Mycology Lab at New York State Department of Health.
For more information, please visit: https://wyss.harvard.edu/news/a-crispr-fingerprint-of-pathogenic-c-auris-fungi/
